summary: Sweden is the largest country in the Nordic region by area, known for its high-welfare society, design brands and the Nobel Prize; it joined NATO in 2024.

ranking.name: Lutheranism (Church of Sweden)
ranking.description: In 1527 King Gustav Vasa broke with the Roman Curia at the Riksdag of Västerås, confiscated church property and introduced Lutheranism; in 1593 the Uppsala Synod formally established the Lutheran faith, and the Church of Sweden became the state church from then on. In the past Swedes automatically became church members at birth, so membership was always high; but since the separation of church and state in 2000, large numbers of people leave the church every year, and the membership share has fallen to about half, with most people coming into contact with the church only at baptisms, weddings and funerals.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: From the 20th century Sweden industrialized and urbanized rapidly, the welfare state took over the social relief and education functions the church had originally provided, and the role of religion in daily life weakened greatly. After the Church of Sweden separated from the state in 2000, leaving the church became even freer, and together with the spread of education and individualist values, Sweden is regarded as one of the most secularized countries in the world.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived mainly with immigrants: in the 1960s–1970s there were laborers from Turkey and Yugoslavia, and from the 1980s refugees from Iran, Iraq, Somalia and Bosnia fleeing the Iran–Iraq War and civil wars. During the European refugee crisis of 2015 Sweden took in large numbers of Syrians and Afghans, and the Muslim population increased further, concentrated mainly in large cities such as Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: After the Reformation Catholicism was banned in Sweden for a long time; the law was gradually relaxed only from the 1860s, and freedom of belief was fully guaranteed only by the 1951 Religious Freedom Act. Today's Catholics are mostly immigrants from Poland, Croatia, Chile, Iraq and elsewhere, and in 2017 Anders Arborelius, Bishop of Stockholm, became Sweden's first cardinal.

religion.background: Sweden changed from the Norse beliefs of the Viking Age to Catholicism in the 11th–12th centuries; in 1527 King Gustav Vasa pushed the Reformation, Lutheranism became the state religion, and state and church were long one. Free church movements appeared in the 19th century, and the law fully guaranteed religious freedom only in 1951. In 2000 the Church of Sweden was separated from the state, and society has already become highly secularized. Waves of immigration from the late 20th century have brought new religious communities such as Islam, Eastern Orthodoxy and Catholicism.

language.official: Swedish is the official language, and five minority languages including Finnish and Sami are also recognized.

ranking.name: Swedish
ranking.description: Swedish belongs to the North Germanic branch and descends from the Old Norse of the Viking Age. The Swedish-language Bible published on the order of Gustav Vasa in 1541 laid the foundation of the written language, and in 1786 King Gustav III founded the Swedish Academy to regulate the language. The 2009 Language Act formally established Swedish as the country's principal language; because Sweden was for a long time an ethnically homogeneous country, the great majority of citizens have it as their mother tongue, and immigrants must also learn it at school.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic speakers are mainly immigrants from Iraq, Lebanon and Palestine since the 1980s, and the large numbers of Syrian refugees who arrived around 2015. Within a few decades it has become one of the most common non-indigenous languages in Sweden, especially in immigrant neighborhoods such as Malmö and the suburbs of Stockholm, and schools also offer mother-tongue instruction.

ranking.name: Finnish
ranking.description: Finland was part of the Kingdom of Sweden until 1809, and the Torne Valley in the north has had Finnish-speaking communities since ancient times; their Meänkieli is also regarded as a separate language. In the 1950s–1970s Finland's economy was weaker, and hundreds of thousands of Finns moved to Sweden to work in factories, forming a large Finnish-speaking community. In 2000 Sweden formally recognized Finnish, Meänkieli, Sami, Romani and Yiddish as the five national minority languages.

language.history: Swedish descends from the Old Norse of the Viking Age; it was first carved in runic letters, and after the introduction of Christianity the Latin alphabet was used. Commercial contact with the medieval Hanseatic League led Swedish to absorb a great deal of Low German vocabulary. The Swedish Bible published in 1541 became the basis of the standard written language, and the Swedish Academy, founded in 1786, is responsible for compiling dictionaries and regulating the language. In the late 20th century immigration brought languages such as Arabic, Persian and Somali, and the 2009 Language Act established Swedish as the principal language and guaranteed the five national minority languages.

ranking.name: Köttbullar (Swedish meatballs)
ranking.description: Small meatballs of mixed ground beef and pork with breadcrumbs, onion and milk, pan-fried and served with cream sauce, lingonberry jam and mashed potatoes.
ranking.history: The recipe for Swedish meatballs first appears in Kajsa Warg's famous cookbook of 1754; at first it was mostly a dish of upper-class households, and only after the meat grinder became common in the 19th century did it become an ordinary family dish. A long-told story is that King Charles XII brought the method of Turkish meatballs back to Sweden during his exile in the Ottoman Empire in 1709–1714, and in 2018 Sweden's official Twitter account also mentioned that meatballs derive from a Turkish recipe. Later IKEA's restaurants in its stores around the world sold meatballs, making them the best-known Swedish food in the world.

ranking.name: Kanelbullar (cinnamon buns)
ranking.description: Fermented dough flavored with cardamom is spread with butter, cinnamon and sugar, rolled up and baked, topped with white pearl sugar, sweet and soft in texture.
ranking.history: Cinnamon buns became common in Sweden only in the 1920s, after World War I, because sugar, butter and white flour had been rationed during the war, and after the war, when supplies returned, this luxurious sweet bread became a treat every household could bake. It is at the core of the Swedish "fika" culture: stopping while working or chatting to have coffee with something sweet is an important social habit. In 1999 the Swedish Home Baking Council set October 4 as "Cinnamon Bun Day."

ranking.name: Semla
ranking.description: A cardamom-flavored round bun with the top cut off and the inside hollowed out, filled with almond paste and whipped cream, with the top put back on and dusted with powdered sugar.
ranking.history: The semla was originally a festival bread eaten on Shrove Tuesday, before the start of the Catholic Lent, and in early times it was eaten in a bowl of hot milk. After the Reformation fasting was no longer strictly observed, but the custom of eating semlor remained. In 1771 King Adolf Frederick is said to have died after eating a large number of semlor following a lavish dinner, a historical anecdote Swedes enjoy telling. Today semlor are sold from New Year until Easter and are the most anticipated dessert of winter.

ranking.name: Surströmming (fermented herring)
ranking.description: Baltic herring is cured with a small amount of salt and left to ferment, then canned; the smell is extremely strong, and it is usually eaten with thin crispbread, potatoes, onion and sour cream.
ranking.history: In the past salt was an expensive import, and coastal inhabitants of northern Sweden cured herring with less salt, letting the fish be preserved through fermentation, which created this unique food, recorded at least as early as the 16th century. The main production area is the "High Coast" in the north, and traditionally the new season's product goes on sale only in late August, accompanied by outdoor "surströmming parties." Because the cans bulge from continued fermentation, some airlines forbid taking them on board, which has also made it one of the world's best-known "smelliest foods."

ranking.name: Smörgåstårta (sandwich cake)
ranking.description: A savory sandwich cake made of layers of white bread filled with shrimp, salmon, egg, mayonnaise and the like, coated on the outside with cream cheese and decorated like a cake.
ranking.history: The smörgåstårta is a fairly young Swedish dish, generally believed to have been introduced and made popular in the 1960s by the pastry chef Gunnar Ekström of the northern city of Östersund. It can be prepared in advance and suits sharing among many guests, so it quickly became a standard dish for house parties. Today it is common at graduations, birthdays, christenings and company gatherings, and Swedish supermarkets sell ready-made sandwich cakes all year round.
